1241.quote_or_event: “O mind, there is only the One medicine, mantra and healing herb - center your consciousness firmly on the One Lord.”
1241.explanation: Guru Nanak speaks directly to his own mind and tells it that there is a single remedy for its sickness: steady remembrance of the One Lord.
1241.tie_back: The Kural's wife begs her heart to think of some medicine, any medicine, for a grief nothing else can cure; Guru Nanak, also addressing the mind, names the one medicine that heals the longing soul.
1241.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 156, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1241._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on the shared device of speaking to one's own mind and asking for the one medicine, though Guru Nanak's sickness is separation from God and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1242.quote_or_event: “I am ungraceful and ill-mannered, full of endless faults. How can I go to enjoy my Husband Lord?”
1242.explanation: In the hymn known as Kuchajji, Guru Nanak speaks as a soul-bride who blames her own faults, not her Husband, for the distance between them.
1242.tie_back: The Kural's wife tells her heart that its pain is folly because he has no love for them; Gurbani turns the charge around, teaching that the divine Husband never lacks love and the gap lies in the bride's own failings.
1242.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 762, Raag Soohee (Kuchajji), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1242._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the bride's lament over a distant Husband but deliberately contrasts with the Kural, since Gurbani never says the Lord lacks love, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1243.quote_or_event: “My body is cooking like an oven; my bones are burning like firewood. If my feet become tired, I will walk on my head, if I can meet my Beloved.”
1243.explanation: Sheikh Farid describes a longing so fierce that he would go to his Beloved even on his head once his feet gave out.
1243.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks her heart why it sits here pining for one who has no tender thought for them; Farid shows the opposite of idle pining, a lover ready to go to the Beloved at any cost.
1243.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 119) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1243._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial fit on the burning ache of separation, though the very next salok (120) gently corrects this self-torment and points to the Beloved within, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1244.quote_or_event: “My eyes long for You; when will I see Your Vision?”
1244.explanation: Guru Arjan voices the soul's eyes as aching for a single sight of the Beloved.
1244.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her eyes, set on seeing him, are eating her alive and asks her heart to take them along; Guru Arjan likewise gives the eyes their own longing for the Beloved's vision.
1244.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1094, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1244._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on eyes tormented by longing to see the Beloved, but it lacks the Kural's image of heart and eyes divided, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1245.quote_or_event: “What sort of love is this, which clings to duality? O Nanak, he alone is called a lover, who remains forever immersed in absorption.”
1245.explanation: Guru Angad teaches that true love does not drift elsewhere when the Beloved seems distant; a real lover stays absorbed in the one Beloved.
1245.tie_back: The Kural's wife decides she cannot give up a husband who does not come, calling him hostile; Guru Angad likewise holds that a true lover never turns away from the Beloved.
1245.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1245._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on constancy in love despite the Beloved's absence, though Guru Angad defines love of God rather than a wife's loyalty, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1246.quote_or_event: “The happy soul-bride knows the worth of her Husband Lord. Renouncing pride, she enjoys peace and pleasure.”
1246.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas says the bride who truly values her Husband lets go of her pride, and so enjoys union with Him.
1246.tie_back: The Kural's wife tells her heart its anger is false, since it melts the moment the beloved embraces them; Ravidas likewise teaches that the bride who knows her Husband's worth drops her pride and enjoys His company.
1246.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 793, Raag Soohee, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1246._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial fit, since Ravidas speaks of giving up ego (haumai) rather than a lover's sham sulking (pulavi), and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1247.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, when you are in love with the One Lord, duality and alienation depart.”
1247.explanation: Kabir says that a heart wholly given to the One Lord is no longer torn between rival pulls.
1247.tie_back: The Kural's wife tells her heart to give up either desire or modesty, because she cannot bear both at once; Kabir offers the Sikh answer to a divided heart, single-minded love that ends the inner tug-of-war.
1247.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1365, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1247._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it addresses a divided heart, but Kabir's 'duality' is love split between God and the world, not the Kural's specific clash of desire and modesty, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1248.quote_or_event: “Thirsty with desire, I wander around; when will I behold the Lord of the World?”
1248.explanation: Guru Arjan pictures the longing soul roaming about in search of the Beloved she cannot yet see.
1248.tie_back: The Kural's wife chides her foolish heart for running after the one who left even as it complains he will not come back in kindness; Guru Arjan's bride likewise wanders in thirsting search of the absent Lord.
1248.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 928, Raag Raamkalee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1248._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on the restless heart that goes after an absent Beloved, though Gurbani does not mock the seeker as the Kural mocks the heart, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1249.quote_or_event: “Fareed, why do you wander from jungle to jungle, crashing through the thorny trees? The Lord abides in the heart; why are you looking for Him in the jungle?”
1249.explanation: Sheikh Farid tells the seeker that the Beloved already lives in the heart, so roaming outside to find Him is pointless.
1249.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks her heart where it is going to look for the beloved who already dwells inside it; Farid asks the very same question of the soul searching the jungles for a Lord who abides within.
1249.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 19) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1249._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); near one-to-one on the paradox of searching outside for a Beloved who lives in the heart, though Farid speaks of God and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1250.quote_or_event: “So smash your bracelets along with your bed, O soul-bride, and break your arms, along with the arms of your couch.”
1250.explanation: Guru Nanak tells the adorned bride whose Husband does not love her that all her ornaments are worthless and might as well be broken.
1250.tie_back: The Kural's wife fears that holding in her heart one who has left her will cost her still more of her beauty; Guru Nanak likewise says that adornment and beauty are wasted when the Husband's love is absent.
1250.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 557, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1250._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the image of a bride's beauty and ornaments ruined in separation, but Guru Nanak's point is that outward adornment cannot win the Lord, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.
